title: The throwaway culture
hookLine: a culture that discards things and people
carry: nothing and no one thrown away
last: GOD HEARS TWO CRIES: THE EARTH'S AND THE POOR'S.

lines: A CROWD FED ON A HILLSIDE.
cards: A hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has just eaten, fed from five barley loaves and two fishes. Everyone is full.

It's time to go home. But Jesus says to his disciples, in the Douay-Rheims: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." So they walk the hillside picking up leftovers, and the baskets fill.
After a miracle of abundance, he cares about the scraps. Pope Francis has a name for the opposite habit, a way of living where whatever is no longer useful gets tossed.

teach.b: Francis calls it the throwaway culture. First, it starts with things. Phones replaced while they still work.
Food bought and binned. Clothes worn twice. In Laudato Si', Francis points out that nature doesn't work like that: in a forest, what falls becomes food for something else.
Human habits, he says, haven't learned that cycle, so waste piles up. Second, it doesn't stay with things.
A culture that gets used to discarding objects slowly gets used to discarding people: whoever isn't productive, isn't convenient, isn't useful right now.

Francis names who tends to be pushed out: the unborn, the elderly, the sick, the poor, migrants. In another letter, The Joy of the Gospel, he says the excluded are no longer even treated as exploited.
They're treated as leftovers. Third, a different way of seeing. Every person, in Catholic teaching, has a dignity that doesn't depend on what they can do.
The baby who can't work, the grandmother who can't remember, the man on the corner with a cardboard sign.
Nobody is a leftover. That's why Francis keeps linking the earth and the person: the eyes that learn to see a broken chair as worth fixing can learn to see a slowed-down neighbor as worth visiting.
Fourth, it's practiced in small things. Repair.
Mend. Eat the leftovers. Visit the one nobody visits.
These look like household tips. Francis treats them as a quiet protest against a whole way of life, an echo of the care on that hillside for crumbs.

how: Catholics respond to Francis's critique of the throwaway culture in practical ways: parish repair cafés and food-rescue projects, visits to the elderly and the sick, and ministries that accompany people others overlook.

o: a habit of discarding things, and then people
an old name for the poor who live on scraps
the trash left behind after a big feast

games.q: the throwaway culture — tap the pairs.

s: Francis's throwaway culture is only about plastic and trash
his sharper point is that discarding things trains us to discard people.
after feeding the crowd, Jesus has the leftovers gathered
"gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost."
in this teaching, a person's dignity depends on being useful
the dignity of every person doesn't depend on what they can do.

games.q: you're a disciple on the hillside. the crowd is fed and full, and crumbs are everywhere. what does Jesus ask?
o: leave the scraps for the birds.
gather up the fragments, so none are lost.
hand out what's left to the next town.
games.why: he tells them to gather the fragments "lest they be lost." after a miracle of plenty, he cares about the scraps.

practice: Think of something at home that's broken or half-used and headed for the trash, a shirt with a loose button, a wobbly chair, food at the back of the fridge, and decide what fixing it, or using it up, would take.

Then let your mind move from things to people: is there someone who has quietly been set aside, someone you haven't called because it's easier not to? If you pray, bring them to God; if you don't, just hold their name for a moment.

wordCard.voice: The throwaway culture. Francis's name for a way of living that discards things, and then people, once they stop being useful. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing and no one thrown away. Back tomorrow, same hill.
